lead: A point estimate gives one number. Interval estimation gives a range of plausible values for an unknown population parameter. The range is random because it is built from a random sample. A 95% confidence interval is made by a rule that traps the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples, in the long run. Engineers use it for mean strength of concrete, average delivery time, proportion of failed UPI payments and variance of a process. Some syllabi call the result an interval estimate.
prereq: You need: point estimation, sampling distributions of the mean and variance, the t and chi-square distributions, and the normal distribution from Unit 3.

sections.h3: The rule and the coverage meaning

blocks.text: A point estimate gives one number. An interval estimator gives two random limits, L and U, built from the sample. After you observe the sample, the limits become two numbers l and u. The confidence coefficient is 1−α. Here α is the total tail probability left outside the interval. For a two-sided interval, α/2 goes in each tail. Common values are 95% (α = 0.05) and 99% (α = 0.01).

blocks.where: θ is the unknown population parameter; L and U are random lower and upper limits; 1−α is the confidence coefficient, such as 0.95.

blocks.text: Coverage is a long-run property of the rule. If you repeat the sampling and interval calculation many times, about 95% of the intervals from a 95% rule contain θ. After one interval is computed, do not say it has 95% probability to contain θ. It either contains θ or it does not; the probability statement belongs to the random limits before the data are seen.

items: A wider interval has higher confidence for the same sample.
A larger n makes the interval narrower.
A prediction interval for one future observation is wider than a confidence interval for a mean.

sections.h3: Mean with known and unknown σ

blocks.text: For a normal population with known σ, the standard error of x̄ is σ/√n. The interval is:

blocks.where: x̄ is the sample mean; σ is the population standard deviation; n is sample size; z<sub>1−α/2</sub> is the normal value with area 1−α/2 to its left. For 95%, z = 1.96.

blocks.text: When σ is unknown, replace σ by s and z by t. The interval is:

blocks.where: s is the sample standard deviation; n−1 is degrees of freedom; t<sub>q,ν</sub> is the t value with area q to its left. For 95% and ν = 15, t = 2.131.

blocks.text: This t interval is exact for a normal population and approximate for large n from other populations. The margin of error is E = critical value × standard error. To plan a sample size for a mean, use n = (z σ / E)², rounded up. Using z instead of t when n is small makes the interval too narrow.
For a normal population, a 100(1−α)% interval for the variance σ² uses the chi-square distribution.

blocks.where: s² is the sample variance; n−1 is degrees of freedom; χ²<sub>p,ν</sub> cuts off area p to its right. The interval for σ is the square root of these limits.

blocks.text: For a large sample and a proportion p, the point estimate is p̂ = X/n, where X is the number with the trait. The interval is:

blocks.where: p̂ is the sample proportion; n is sample size; the normal approximation needs n p̂ and n(1−p̂) to be at least about 5 to 10.

blocks.text: Use this proportion interval only when the counts are large enough. For small counts, exact or score intervals are better. The margin of error again is critical value × standard error. For planning a proportion sample size, use n = z² p(1−p)/E², with a guessed p; p = 0.5 is the safe worst case.

figure.caption: The sample gives a point estimate and a standard error; the t critical value turns the standard error into a margin of error, and the interval is the estimate plus or minus that margin. The numbers are from the worked example.

spec.title: Building a confidence interval
spec.aria: Sample data gives a point estimate, then a standard error, then a critical value, then the margin of error and the interval.

examples.question: A random sample of n = 16 from a normal population gives x̄ = 52 and s = 8. The population standard deviation σ is unknown. Find a 95% confidence interval for the population mean μ. Use the t table.
steps: The parameter is μ. σ is unknown and n = 16 is small, so use the t interval, not z.
For 95% confidence, α = 0.05 and α/2 = 0.025. The left-tail area is 1 − α/2 = 0.975. From the t table, t<sub>0.975,15</sub> = 2.131.
Margin of error = t × standard error = 2.131 × 2 = 4.262.
examples.answer: The 95% confidence interval for μ is (47.738, 56.262), about (47.74, 56.26).
examples.check:
import math
n = 16
xbar = 52.0
s = 8.0
tcrit = 2.131
se = s / math.sqrt(n)
me = tcrit * se
low = xbar - me
high = xbar + me
print(round(se, 3))
print(round(me, 3))
print(round(low, 3))
print(round(high, 3))

traps: Using z instead of t when σ is unknown and n is small; this makes the interval too narrow.
Saying the observed interval has 95% probability to contain μ. Coverage is the long-run fraction of intervals from the rule, not a probability for one fixed interval.
Swapping the two chi-square denominators in a variance interval. The lower limit uses the larger chi-square value, so the lower limit stays below the upper limit.
Rounding the planned sample size down. Round up, otherwise the margin of error can exceed the target E.
Using the normal proportion interval when n p̂ or n(1−p̂) is small; the normal approximation is poor there.

quiz.q: Define the confidence coefficient 1−α and state what α is.
quiz.a: 1−α is the long-run fraction of intervals from the rule that contain the parameter. α is the total tail probability outside a two-sided interval, with α/2 in each tail.

quiz.q: Why is it wrong to say a computed 95% confidence interval (47.7, 56.3) has probability 0.95 to contain μ?
quiz.a: After the sample is observed, the limits are fixed numbers and μ is fixed. The interval either contains μ or not. The 0.95 belongs to the random procedure that produced the limits, not to this one interval.

quiz.q: A normal population has known σ = 10. A sample of n = 25 gives x̄ = 120. Find a 95% confidence interval for μ using z = 1.96.
A normal sample has n = 10, x̄ = 30 and s = 5. σ is unknown. Use t = 2.262 for 95% confidence. Find the interval for μ.
Two intervals are made from the same sample: a 90% interval and a 99% interval. Which is wider, and why?
quiz.a: The 99% interval is wider. A higher confidence coefficient needs a larger critical value, so the margin of error is larger for the same standard error.

quiz.q: In a sample of n = 400, 140 units have a trait, so p̂ = 0.35. Find a 95% confidence interval for p using z = 1.96.
A report says the 95% confidence interval for mean delivery time is (28, 34) minutes. Give the correct interpretation.
quiz.a: The rule that produced this interval gives intervals containing the true mean in 95% of repeated samples. It does not mean 95% of deliveries take between 28 and 34 minutes, and it is not a 95% probability statement for this fixed interval.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real projects often use bootstrap intervals when no simple formula exists: resample the data many times and take the middle 95% of estimates. Bayesian work reports credible intervals, which have a direct posterior probability statement under a prior. Quality engineers use tolerance intervals for the spread of individual parts and prediction intervals for one future reading. Search next for 'bootstrap confidence interval', 'Wilson score interval' and 'prediction interval versus confidence interval'.
